summary: Barstow sits at the confluence of Interstates 15 and 40 in the Mojave Desert, which means roughly half the traffic between Los Angeles and Las Vegas funnels through its gas stations and drive-throughs — yet the city itself is home to fewer than 25,000 people spread across a sprawling 41 square miles, giving it a density closer to a rural outpost than a freeway hub. That geographic position has made logistics and distribution a genuine employment anchor: massive warehouse and rail operations, including a major BNSF Railway yard, provide jobs that don't require a long commute, and nearby Fort Irwin — the Army's National Training Center — pumps additional economic activity into the area. Housing is strikingly cheap by California standards, with a median home value around $222,600 against a median household income of roughly $51,800, producing a price-to-income ratio under 4.3 — a figure that would be fantasy in most of coastal California — though a 23.2% poverty rate signals that affordability here reflects limited economic bandwidth, not hidden bargains. The climate is unambiguous desert: 10.6 hours of daily sunshine on average, summer highs that routinely scorch past 100°F, and mild winters that make December through March the most comfortable stretch. The Mojave River bisects the city in a broad, usually dry wash, and the terrain is flat desert floor ringed by low, sunbaked mountains that deliver wide-open sunset panoramas but almost no shade. Barstow is a place where California's vastness is the dominant daily fact — more sky and highway than sidewalk, more passing-through energy than staying-put infrastructure.
